title: This gristle throbs
gist: Philip Clark reports on an ICA talk marking 50 years since Throbbing Gristle's first London gig at the 1976 Prostitution exhibition, where Cosey Fanni Tutti and Chris Carter reminisced. He argues the band's music endures because concept and sound were perfectly aligned in exploring hidden sounds.

insights.claim: A 1976 ICA exhibition called Prostitution, around which Throbbing Gristle played their first London gig, prompted Tory MP Nicholas Fairbairn to call the musicians 'wreckers of civilisation'.
insights.speaker: Philip Clark

insights.claim: Throbbing Gristle's ICA performance was meant only as a backdrop to the exhibition but made such an impact that it became COUM Transmissions' last outing.
insights.speaker: Philip Clark
insights.so_what: Origin story of an influential band.

insights.claim: Cosey Fanni Tutti said she felt uncomfortable 'being part of history while still being alive' amid a retrospective music culture that feasts on reissues and anniversaries.
insights.speaker: Philip Clark
insights.so_what: Reflects the commercial weight of reissue and anniversary markets in music.
insights.quote: being part of history while still being alive

insights.claim: Chris Carter said his sense of sound outside music came from working as a TV sound engineer and from the BBC Radiophonic Workshop and The Goon Show, encountering avant-garde composers only in retrospect.
insights.speaker: Philip Clark
insights.so_what: Context on non-traditional pathways into electronic music.

insights.claim: Throbbing Gristle rejected song form, combining improvisation, drones, drum machines, tape loops and synthesisers into intentionally abrasive sound; Tutti considered TG separate from punk despite frequent categorisation as punk or industrial.
insights.speaker: Philip Clark

insights.claim: Clark argues Throbbing Gristle's music retains its power because concept and sound ran in perfect alignment as they explored usually hidden sounds.
insights.speaker: Philip Clark

insights.claim: Throbbing Gristle's first incarnation ended in 1981, they reunited for six years from 2004, and the band ended with the deaths of Christopherson in 2010 and P-Orridge in 2020.
insights.speaker: Philip Clark
